segments.text: Welcome to First Principles Daily, episode 50 for July 25th, 2026.
Let's break something down to its raw materials and build the reasoning back up.
Rail moves a ton of mile with far less energy than trucks, yet the cheaper physics modes
still loses on delivered cost.
A truck burns several times more fuel than a locomotive to move the same ton, the same distance.
Yet trucks still handle the majority of ton miles across much of North America.
The difference traces directly to rolling resistance.
Steel wheels on steel rails deform far less than rubber tires on asphalt, so the energy
required to overcome friction drops sharply.
That physical gap sets a floor well below current truck rates.
The distance between that floor and what shippers actually pay is the opening for redesign.
The surprise is not that rail is more efficient in a laboratory sense.
The surprise is that the efficiency advantage survives real-world operations yet still fails
to capture most volume once every handling step and schedule constraint is counted.
Trucking grew dominant because it offers door-to-door service without transfers.
A shipper loads a trailer at the factory dock and the same trailer arrives at the customer
dock.
Often on a schedule the shipper controls.
Rail requires the freight to reach a terminal.
The freight must be lifted or rolled onto a flat car or into a box car.
It moves in blocks that follow fixed timetables.
Then it is unloaded and transferred again at the far end.
Each of those handoffs adds labor, equipment time, and delay.
The delay compounds into carrying cost penalties for the cargo itself.
The sequence begins with drainage from origin to the first rail terminal.
It continues through classification and blocking inside the yard.
It proceeds along the main line under dispatcher control.
It ends with another drainage leg after the container or trailer is set off.
Every transition point introduces both direct expense and uncertainty about arrival windows.
Regulation and right-of-way rules further widen the gap.
Trucking operates on publicly funded highways whose maintenance costs are only partly recovered
through fuel taxes.
Railroads must maintain their own track and pay property taxes on it.
Class wine railroads therefore price services to cover both the variable cost of moving trains
and the fixed cost of the network.
This pricing pushes published rates above the energy floor.
Trucking rates embed driver wages, fuel, equipment depreciation, and the cost of empty backhalls.
Those backhalls arise because truck routes are point-to-point rather than corridor-based.
The public road subsidy appears as lower marginal cost per mile once the vehicle is already on the pavement.
Fragmented ownership adds another layer.
Thousands of independent carriers compete on the highway.
This competition keeps marginal rates fluid.
Rail capacity is concentrated in a handful of networks whose schedules and equipment pools must be coordinated across multiple owners.
The result is that even when rail fuel efficiency is three to four times better per tonne mile,
the total delivered cost for many shipments remains lower by truck.
That outcome holds once first mile pickup, last mile delivery, and schedule reliability are included.
Some shippers already accept rail for its lower line haul rate.
Those shippers typically move bulk commodities whose time sensitivity is low enough to absorb the added variability.
Most manufactured goods stay on trucks.
A rough magic wand estimate starts with the energy difference alone.
Moving one tonne one mile by rail requires on the order of one third to one quarter the fuel energy needed by truck.
Rolling resistance on steel is roughly 0.001 to 0.002 times the normal force, while truck tires run closer to 0.01.
Diesel fuel contains about 130 megajoules per gallon.
The direct energy cost for rail sits well below 1 cent per tonne mile at current commodity prices.
The truck figure is several times higher before any other expenses are added.
If the only variable were propulsion energy, the floor would be set almost entirely by that ratio.
The arithmetic shows that even modest improvements in terminal handling could bring total cost close to the energy component alone.
That energy floor is only the starting point.
The finished price of truck freight today is reported in the range of 5 to 10 cents per tonne mile for typical over the road moves.
Dividing that finished price by the raw energy component produces an idiot index on the order of 5 to 10 when only fuel is counted.
The index climbs much higher once terminal handling, driver time, empty miles, and regulatory overhead are treated as process costs rather than material costs.
The gap is therefore not in the steel or the diesel itself.
The gap sits in the sequence of transfers, the scheduling rigidity, and the capital tied up in assets that sit idle between loads.
Consider a 500 mile lane to make the index concrete.
The energy portion might represent roughly one-tenth of the total invoice.
The remaining 9 tenths cover the labor and equipment time spent before and after the line haul segment.
The largest single addition comes from first and last mile operations.
A typical intermodal move may spend 30 to 50 percent of its total cost on drainage to and from the rail terminal.
That segment is only a small fraction of the total distance.
Terminal dwell time and equipment repositioning add further layers.
Containers and trailers must be sorted, lifted, and sometimes stored.
Each step requires specialized machinery and labor whose utilization is limited by arrival patterns rather than continuous flow.
Schedule inflexibility compounds the carrying cost of the freight itself.
Shippers hold inventory buffers to cover the variability between rail cutoff times and actual delivery.
A redesign would begin by collapsing the first and last mile penalty through denser networks of smaller,
automated, transload points rather than a few large classification yards.
If standardized containers could be transferred with minimal human intervention,
handling cost per tonn mile would fall closer to the energy floor.
Short trains or even individual cars could be dispatched on demand.
Electrification of the line haul segment would then remove diesel price volatility.
That step works provided the capital cost of catenary or battery systems could be
amortized over high utilization. Each avoided dry edge mile removes both fuel and driver time.
Each reduced dwell hour frees equipment for another revenue move.
Autonomy changes the math on the truck side as well.
Driver wages currently represent 30-40% of many truck operating costs.
Removing the driver reduces that component.
The physics of rolling resistance remains unchanged.
The opportunity therefore lies in hybrid networks where autonomous trucks feed automated rail corridors
for the long middle segment.
The transfer points themselves must be engineered for near zero dwell.
The automated transfer hardware would have to handle the existing container fleet
without custom adapters. Dispatch algorithms would have to match arrival patterns to available
rail slots in real time. Regulatory approval for mixed use corridors would have to be obtained
without decade-long environmental reviews. The hard constraints are capital intensity and network
effects. Building new transload facilities or electrifying existing lines requires large up
front outlays. Returns depend on volume commitments that shippers are reluctant to give until
the service is already reliable. Right-of-way acquisition or shared use agreements with passenger
operators add regulatory and political friction that cannot be engineered away.
Any serious attempt must therefore start with existing corridors and existing container standards.
The goal is improving utilization and transfer speed before new infrastructure is contemplated.
Railroads already invest in intermodal terminals. Those investments still treat the terminal
as a batch processing node rather than a continuous flow interface.
The idiot index remains largely intact. The real cost of freight is set by how many times the cargo
must stop and change hands. It is not set by the fuel burned while the cargo is moving.
When those stops are treated as fixed features of the system rather than variables to be engineered
down, the price stays far above the energy floor. The physics has been known for more than a century.
Standardization only creates leverage when the interfaces are cheap and fast.
A container is useless if every transfer still requires a crane, a clerk, and a half-day of dwell.
The first concrete signal that someone is attacking this problem would be a measurable drop in average
terminal dwell time on a single corridor. That drop would need to be achieved without adding new
